faq.q: Why is O‑negative considered the safest emergency blood?

exam: A 28‑year‑old pregnant woman with unknown blood type presents with postpartum hemorrhage — what blood should you give first and why? — Give O‑negative blood; it avoids ABO and Rh incompatibility while definitive typing is arranged.

A patient with sickle cell disease has a history of multiple transfusions and now needs a unit; how do you ensure compatibility? — Perform extended phenotyping or antibody screen; if unavailable, use least antigen‑mismatched blood and monitor closely.

You receive a cross‑match report showing ‘compatible’ but the patient develops fever and dark urine within 30 minutes — what is the most likely cause and next step? — Acute hemolytic reaction; stop transfusion, give IV fluids, and order a DAT.
Explain why a Rh‑negative mother with an Rh‑positive fetus should receive anti‑D immunoglobulin — to prevent maternal sensitisation that could cause hemolytic disease in future pregnancies.

In a rural clinic without a laboratory, a child with severe anemia needs transfusion; what bedside test can you use and what are its limits? — Use a point‑of‑care ABO strip; it only determines ABO, not antibodies or Rh, so give O‑negative blood and arrange formal typing later.

A patient on antimalarial therapy develops a sudden drop in hemoglobin after transfusion; what differential diagnoses should you consider? — Acute hemolytic reaction, malaria‑related hemolysis, or drug‑induced immune hemolysis; check DAT and review medication.
Why is reverse typing essential even after a clear forward type? — It detects unexpected antibodies and confirms the forward result, reducing risk of missed incompatibility.

During a massive transfusion protocol, why is it important to monitor for citrate toxicity and how does it relate to blood typing? — Citrate binds calcium causing hypocalcaemia; while unrelated to typing, it is a critical safety issue during large volume transfusion.
ai.title: Blood Typing and Transfusion Compatibility
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Blood typing determines ABO and Rh status to guide safe transfusion and prevent hemolytic reactions. In low‑resource settings, simple bedside methods and limited lab resources shape decision‑making.

b: ABO antigens are carbohydrate structures on the red cell membrane.
Rh factor is a protein antigen; Rh‑positive patients have D antigen, Rh‑negative do not.
sections.p: Blood typing identifies the antigens on red cells (ABO) and the presence of the D antigen (Rh). The result predicts which donor blood will be compatible and which antibodies may cause hemolysis.

t.b: What is the patient's ABO/Rh group? – Positive agglutination indicates presence of the corresponding antigen.

t.a: Reverse (serum) typing – tube or slide method
t.b: Does the patient have anti‑A or anti‑B antibodies? – Agglutination with known cells confirms antibody presence, confirming the forward result.
Is the patient Rh‑positive? – Agglutination means D antigen present; no agglutination means Rh‑negative.
Is donor blood compatible with the patient? – No hemolysis after mixing patient serum with donor cells suggests compatibility.

b: Anti‑A and anti‑B are naturally occurring IgM; they cause immediate intravascular hemolysis.
Anti‑D is usually IgG; it can cross the placenta and cause HDN.
The most severe incompatibility is O‑negative donor to A‑positive recipient.
sections.p: Understanding the immunology of ABO and Rh systems helps predict transfusion reactions and manage hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN).

b: Mass casualty or obstetric hemorrhage: use O‑negative blood for Rh‑negative women and O‑positive for men or Rh‑positive women.
Sickle cell disease crises: patients often have allo‑antibodies; extended phenotyping may be needed.
HIV/TB/malaria patients: no impact on ABO, but transfusion‑transmitted infections remain a risk; screen donors carefully.
sections.p: In emergencies, knowing a patient’s blood type guides rapid transfusion decisions, especially where full cross‑matching is delayed.

t.b: Can I quickly confirm ABO in a remote clinic? – Positive line indicates antigen presence; if unavailable, rely on donor O‑negative blood.
Is there immune hemolysis after transfusion? – Positive DAT suggests antibody‑mediated red cell destruction.

b: Always state the four major incompatibilities (A→B, B→A, O→A/B/AB, Rh‑negative → Rh‑positive).
Explain why O‑negative is the universal donor and AB‑positive the universal recipient.
Describe steps when a cross‑match is unavailable: give O‑negative, monitor for hemolysis, arrange definitive typing ASAP.
sections.p: Examiners test reasoning about compatibility, emergency transfusion, and interpretation of mismatched results.

sections.p: Errors often arise from assuming ABO compatibility without confirming Rh status or from misreading weak reactions.

whenToSeekHelp: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction – fever, chills, dark urine, hypotension, back pain.
Severe allergic reaction – urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension.
Delayed hemolysis – falling hemoglobin 7‑10 days after transfusion with jaundice.
